_about: Plain-language, jurisdiction-aware explanations of what each clause type does, for a non-lawyer reading an Indian commercial contract. Used verbatim by the extractive advisory backend.
INDEMNITY: An indemnity is a promise to cover the other side's losses if certain things go wrong. Check who indemnifies whom, what triggers it, whether there is a monetary cap, and whether it is limited to third-party claims.
LIMITATION_OF_LIABILITY: This clause caps how much one or both parties can be made to pay if the contract goes wrong, and often excludes indirect losses. Check the cap amount and whether it is the same for both sides.
TERMINATION: This sets out when and how each party can end the contract, and what happens on exit. Check whether the rights are balanced, the notice periods, and payment obligations on termination.
RENEWAL: This determines whether the contract ends on its term date or rolls over automatically. If renewal is automatic, note the deadline for opting out.
PAYMENT: This covers fees, invoicing, payment timelines, taxes and interest on late payment. Check the payment window, the default-interest rate, and whether amounts are inclusive or exclusive of GST.
CONFIDENTIALITY: This restricts how each side may use and share the other's non-public information. Check what counts as confidential, how long the duty lasts, and the permitted disclosures.
GOVERNING_LAW: This picks the law that governs how the contract is interpreted. For an Indian contract this is usually Indian law.
DISPUTE_RESOLUTION: This sets the steps for resolving disagreements, often negotiation then mediation then arbitration or court.
ARBITRATION: This sends disputes to a private arbitrator instead of the courts. Check the seat (which decides the supervising courts), the number of arbitrators, the rules, and the language.
JURISDICTION: This names the courts that can hear disputes. It matters for where you would have to litigate and can be inconvenient if it is far from you.
FORCE_MAJEURE: This excuses a party from performing when something outside its control - disaster, war, epidemic, government action - prevents performance. Check which events are covered and what happens if the event drags on.
INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY: This decides who owns what is created under the contract and what each side keeps. Check when ownership transfers and whether it is tied to payment.
DATA_PROTECTION: This allocates responsibility for personal data and compliance with data-protection law, including India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
NON_COMPETE: This tries to stop a party from competing during or after the contract. In India, post-term non-compete restrictions are frequently unenforceable as a restraint of trade.
NON_SOLICITATION: This restricts poaching the other side's staff or customers. Check the duration and whether general job adverts are carved out.
WARRANTY: These are promises about quality, authority or the state of things. Check what is promised and what warranties are excluded.
ASSIGNMENT: This controls whether either party can transfer its rights and obligations to someone else. Check whether consent is needed and any carve-out for group companies or a sale of business.
NOTICES: This sets how formal notices must be sent and when they count as received. Getting the method wrong can invalidate a termination or claim.
ENTIRE_AGREEMENT: This says the written contract is the whole deal and side promises do not count. Make sure anything you were told or relied on is actually written into the contract.
AMENDMENT: This requires changes to be made in a particular way, usually in writing and signed by both sides.
SEVERABILITY: This keeps the rest of the contract alive if one clause turns out to be invalid.
SCOPE_OF_WORK: This defines what is actually being delivered. Vague scope is a common source of disputes; check it is specific enough.
PARTIES: This identifies who is bound by the contract and their official details. Check the legal names, entity types and addresses are correct, since notices and enforcement depend on them.
